prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first, but after reading all eight ballots I move the optical lattice clock to the top of my preferred configuration. It is the only shortlisted entry ranked by every member, and six of eight put it in their top three. On the merits it is exactly the kind of work I respect: a new measurement method (magic-wavelength trapping removes the lattice light shift while many atoms are interrogated at once) that changed what can be measured. Katori conceived and first demonstrated it and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 level and into many-body clock physics. Independent confirmation is extensive (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others, several species), comparisons agree, and the applications are concrete: tests of constants and relativity, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter searches and the pending redefinition of the second. As a detector builder I know how much calibration and systematics control sits behind a claimed 10^-18 number, and that is what makes this result credible. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the list, which matters for a prize that can credit at most three people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier clock-related prizes: Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency comb) and Wineland (2012, ion control and ion clocks). A reader could say this is an instrument-level step downstream of prizes already given, and that metrology is being rewarded for a refinement rather than a new phenomenon. There is also a timing argument that the committee might prefer to wait until the SI second is actually redefined, and the credit boundary with Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd, Hollberg and the ion-clock community is not perfectly sharp. Finally, I am an astroparticle experimentalist and not an AMO specialist, so I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for the physics of the lattice-clock chronology.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first for its original magic-wavelength idea plus a decisive leap in precision to 10^-18, with a fair two-person split, and flags the open question of whether it is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the case and I think her caveat is the right one to test, but I do not find it fatal. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool for optical frequency measurement and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks. Neither recognised the idea of interrogating a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, which is what gives the stability and the many-atom regime. That is a distinct conceptual step. I would ask her and Kroll to confirm in round 2 that the chronology of Katori's 2003 proposal and early Sr demonstrations versus Ye's record accuracy is firm, since I am taking that from the ballots and not from my own expertise.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Event Horizon Telescope first as a clear, public discovery that turns black holes into something nature lets us look at, and has IceCube third with Halzen and Karle as a clean pair.
responses.response: I put B052 second on my own opening ballot, so I share his enthusiasm for the measurement craft, but I want to qualify the claim that the credit problem is merely hard. The EHT is a collaboration of hundreds, and Falcke, Doeleman and Zensus each represent a different strand (concept, instrument, organisation) with imaging-algorithm and station leaders left out. By contrast the clock has two clearly decisive names. On maturity, I also note that the shadow-size inference remains somewhat model dependent. I would keep EHT as a strong alternative, and I would not equate his first place with scientific superiority over the clock.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first and the optical lattice clock second, noting that priority details (Lemonde, Takamoto) and the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes need discussion, and that the pending redefinition of the second may bear on timing.
responses.response: On timing I disagree gently. Waiting for the formal redefinition would tie a physics judgement to a metrology-body schedule, while the underlying science (many independent 10^-18 clocks, agreeing comparisons) is already confirmed. I accept his point that Lemonde and Takamoto should be examined; if a better-informed colleague argues that one of them is a decisive third contributor, I would want to hear it. I also note his own caution about a close neighbour to the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize, which is a reason I am less drawn to B001 than to the clock this year.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the Higgs discovery with ATLAS and CMS first as the experimental counterpart of the 2013 theory prize, with the difficulty being which three of four names represent two collaborations of thousands.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously, since it is fully mature and confirmed by two independent experiments, and as a particle-physics-trained experimentalist I respect it. My difficulty is the attribution: the choice of three from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee necessarily leaves out one credible leader and balances ATLAS and CMS imperfectly, and Danielsson and Olsson already disagree on the triple. That makes it hard to reach a configuration the committee can defend. I would not rule it out and would be glad to hear whether she sees a principled way to choose the names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the atomic-physics members agree on Katori's priority and the role of Ye's group.

Whether IceCube (Halzen and Karle) deserves a place instead of, or beside, the clock, given the credit questions (AMANDA, other IceCube founders and leaders) that none of us can fully resolve from the supplied text.
Whether a two-part prize combining a clock part with another achievement is needed or whether the single clean two-person award is better.
I have not independently verified the clock priority chronology or the exact precision records; I rely on colleagues' ballots.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred clock configuration. For transparency, my own work is in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and I am an astroparticle physicist, so my opening first choice (IceCube) and EHT lie close to my field; I have no known personal or institutional tie to Halzen, Karle, the EHT leaders, Katori or Ye in my profile.
